GPS Triangle World Masters, Oschatz 2026

This is a coaching analysis of Bill Maisey's (Anglesey MAC) performance at the World Masters, Sport class, Oschatz 2026 - 38 pilots over 17 rounds, where Bill finished 22nd. It is built entirely from the public rcmodelspot GPS telemetry: every pilot's roughly 1 Hz track is recorded, so each round is compared like for like against the pilot who led Bill's own heat group and flew the same air, rather than against the overall winner in different conditions.

  • Performance Analysis

    Round by round against the same-air leader in each heat, decomposed by flight phase - cruise, climb, start and turns - and read against the day's conditions.

  • Recommendations

    The training actions that follow from the evidence, in priority order, with drills, further analysis, resources and rules-legal live-signal options.

  • Innovations

    The art of the possible for coaching technology, from a post-flight AI coach to a navigator heads-up display, each weighed against the Sport-class rules.

Performance Analysis

Bill flew a clean, consistent World Masters and finished mid-field. The data points to one dominant lever and a clear order behind it: this overview sets out the headline, ranks the phases where laps are lost, then separates conditions and week-long form from underlying skill. Every figure is drawn from his own flights against the same-air leader each round.

  • All 17 rounds at a glance: Bill vs round winner vs event winner, against the day's lift
  • 22nd of 38 (12,562 pts); the gap is almost all distance-task
  • Biggest lever: cruise speed between thermals
  • Relatively stronger when thermals are strong
  • Progression separates skill from conditions
  • High ceiling; the fastest gain is raising the floor

Performance summary - every round at a glance

Collapseback to top

Point. Across all 17 rounds Bill (green) sits below his same-air round winner (blue) on score, laps and cruise speed, while matching everyone at the start gate. The gap tracks the day's lift, and event winner Florian Griese (grey) marks the benchmark - though from his own group, not Bill's air.

What to do. Use this as the map for the rest of the overview: the cruise-pace and weak-lift levers below are what closes the laps gap, and the entry-gate charts confirm the start is already competitive. Round winner is Bill's same-air group leader (fair, same-conditions); the event winner flew a different group, so his absolute laps and speed reflect his own air. Per-round scores and laps: event results (rcmodelspot); conditions from Open-Meteo ERA5.

Headline result

Collapseback to top

Point. Bill finished 22nd of 38 on 12,562 points, 2,887 behind winner Florian Griese. Almost the entire gap is the distance task; his landings and rule compliance were faultless all week.

What to do. The training focus is lap count in the distance task, not tidying up landings or avoiding penalties - those are already maxed. The next section ranks the phases that cost the laps, feeding the recommendations. Full standings: event results (rcmodelspot).

Where the ground is lost - phase levers

Collapseback to top

Point. In cost order the levers are cruise speed → climb quality → entry speed → turns. Cruise pace dominates; turns are already close to a strength.

What to do. Train fastest-first: cruise pace between thermals (the ~2.7-lap pace effect), then climb quality for weak-lift days, then a cheap win by using the entry-speed cap; turns and lines are the smallest lever. He matched the leader lap-for-lap in Rounds 7 and 17, so the ceiling is there. The 120 km/h entry cap and scoring are set in the Sport-class regulations; field data from the event results.

Conditions dependence

Collapseback to top

Point. Wind shows no association with Bill's relative standing, but thermal strength does: his normalised score tracks solar radiation (Spearman ρ ≈ +0.61) and his lap count tracks it too (ρ ≈ +0.52). His weakest relative rounds cluster in weak, late-day lift.

What to do. He is competitive when lift is strong and slips when it is scarce, which points the same way as climb quality: weak-lift persistence is the condition-specific fix. Read this as suggestive only - n ≈ 14 distance rounds, not a significance claim. Weather from Open-Meteo ERA5, flights from the event results.

Progression across the week

Collapseback to top

Point. Splitting conditions from skill, there is no clear week-long practice trend. Both series swing round to round with the air; his two strongest normalised results (Rounds 7 and 17) are a first-day and a last-day flight, not the ends of a rising line.

What to do. Round-to-round conditions dominate the record far more than any drift in form, so read single rounds cautiously and judge progress on the conditions-controlled score, not on laps. With n ≈ 14 the trend signal is weak either way. Per-round scores: event results (rcmodelspot).

Consistency - floor vs ceiling

Collapseback to top

Point. The score is dragged down by a few weak-lift rounds, not by the good ones falling short. The two bombouts sit far below the median; his best rounds nearly match the leader.

What to do. A bombout costs more than a strong round gains, so the fastest ranking win is raising the floor - staying aloft through weak, scratchy lift - rather than chasing the ceiling. This is the weak-lift climb work again, seen from the results side. Round scores: event results (rcmodelspot).

Energy Management

Collapseback to top

Point. The altitude panel shows how the energy budget was spent; the speed panel shows the cruise line between climbs. Evidence. Bill recovers about 1075 m of climb against the leader's 1253 m, working off a floor near 148 m, while his speed trace sits below the leader's between thermals. Explain. Less height banked per climb plus a slower cruise drains the glide budget sooner, and the lap count follows.

Ground track & course

Collapseback to top

Point. The traces show where each pilot left the course to climb and how tightly they cornered. Evidence. Bill's thermalling loops sit off the course line while his turnpoint arcs run close to the leader's. Explain. Turnpoint technique is near a strength; the loops, not the corners, are where the height - and the time - go, so wider, slower circles cost most.

Cumulative laps vs leader

Expandback to top

Point. The gap opens gradually, not in one blow-up. Evidence. The leader's step line pulls steadily clear, reaching 10 laps at 34.1 km/h while Bill holds 24.9 km/h for 7. Explain. A slower average lap - mostly slower cruise between thermals - compounds over the task into the 3-lap shortfall.

Biggest-loss segment

Expandback to top

Single biggest-loss window: 9:31-10:31 (60 s). Leader gained 2 lap(s) here while Bill held station (slow lap / weak line).

This is the steepest part of the divergence on the cumulative-laps and Energy Management charts above: one weak segment where the leader banked a clean lap and Bill did not. Recovering even half of these windows across the week is worth roughly a lap a round. Source: event results.

What to train from this round

Expandback to top

The gap here is cruise pace between thermals - the biggest lever overall. Focus on faster inter-thermal cruise, with free opening-lap energy available from a fuller entry speed.

Energy Management

Collapseback to top

Point. The sprint is won on how much speed the height buys, not on staying aloft. Evidence. Both traces bleed altitude for pace across the one lap; Bill averaged 109.1 km/h to Ralph Losemann's 156.4 km/h on the speed panel. Explain. A cleaner high-energy entry and a faster glide line convert more of the same start height into lap speed - the same cruise lever as the distance rounds, isolated to one run.

Ground track & course

Collapseback to top

Point. On the sprint the only line that matters is the racing line through the turnpoints. Evidence. Both traces hug the course triangle with no off-course loops; the corner arcs and start-line crossing sit on the plotted course. Explain. With no lift to hunt, tighter corners and a straighter run between turnpoints are the only time on offer - it comes down to carried speed.

Single-lap speed task

Expandback to top

Point. There is no lap count to build on a sprint - it is decided on the single lap. Evidence. Bill ran 109.1 km/h to Ralph Losemann's 156.4 km/h for 695 points and 29th of 38 on the event results. Explain. The sprint reward is raw pace and a full-energy entry, not endurance, so the lever is top-end cruise speed rather than lasting the distance.

Where the time went

Expandback to top

Speed-run: leader 47 km/h faster on the single run. On a one-lap speed task the whole gap is the single run - there is no in-flight window to isolate, so the single-lap speed panel on the dashboard carries the story. Source: event results.

What to train from this round

Expandback to top

The sprint reward is raw pace and a full-energy start. Train top-end cruise speed and use more of the entry-speed allowance - Bill leaves a large slice of the 120 km/h cap unused.

Energy Management

Collapseback to top

Point. The sprint is won on how much speed the height buys, not on staying aloft. Evidence. Both traces bleed altitude for pace across the one lap; Bill averaged 112.8 km/h to Benjamin Dähn's 153.3 km/h on the speed panel. Explain. A cleaner high-energy entry and a faster glide line convert more of the same start height into lap speed - the same cruise lever as the distance rounds, isolated to one run.

Ground track & course

Collapseback to top

Point. On the sprint the only line that matters is the racing line through the turnpoints. Evidence. Both traces hug the course triangle with no off-course loops; the corner arcs and start-line crossing sit on the plotted course. Explain. With no lift to hunt, tighter corners and a straighter run between turnpoints are the only time on offer - it comes down to carried speed.

Single-lap speed task

Expandback to top

Point. There is no lap count to build on a sprint - it is decided on the single lap. Evidence. Bill ran 112.8 km/h to Benjamin Dähn's 153.3 km/h for 735 points and 29th of 38 on the event results. Explain. The sprint reward is raw pace and a full-energy entry, not endurance, so the lever is top-end cruise speed rather than lasting the distance.

Where the time went

Expandback to top

Speed-run: leader 40 km/h faster on the single run. On a one-lap speed task the whole gap is the single run - there is no in-flight window to isolate, so the single-lap speed panel on the dashboard carries the story. Source: event results.

What to train from this round

Expandback to top

The sprint reward is raw pace and a full-energy start. Train top-end cruise speed and use more of the entry-speed allowance - Bill leaves a large slice of the 120 km/h cap unused.

Energy Management

Collapseback to top

Point. The altitude panel shows how the energy budget was spent; the speed panel shows the cruise line between climbs. Evidence. Bill recovers about 1494 m of climb against the leader's 1826 m, working off a floor near 152 m, while his speed trace sits below the leader's between thermals. Explain. Less height banked per climb plus a slower cruise drains the glide budget sooner, and the lap count follows.

Ground track & course

Collapseback to top

Point. The traces show where each pilot left the course to climb and how tightly they cornered. Evidence. Bill's thermalling loops sit off the course line while his turnpoint arcs run close to the leader's. Explain. Turnpoint technique is near a strength; the loops, not the corners, are where the height - and the time - go, so wider, slower circles cost most.

Cumulative laps vs leader

Expandback to top

Point. The gap opens gradually, not in one blow-up. Evidence. The leader's step line pulls steadily clear, reaching 13 laps at 44.8 km/h while Bill holds 44.6 km/h for 13. Explain. A slower average lap - mostly slower cruise between thermals - compounds over the task into the 0-lap shortfall.

Biggest-loss segment

Expandback to top

Single biggest-loss window: 5:00-6:00 (60 s). Leader gained 1 lap(s) here while Bill was thermalling low (climbed +47 m).

This is the steepest part of the divergence on the cumulative-laps and Energy Management charts above: one weak segment where the leader banked a clean lap and Bill did not. Recovering even half of these windows across the week is worth roughly a lap a round. Source: event results.

What to train from this round

Expandback to top

Round 17 is a near-win: Bill matched Jens Geider lap-for-lap for 999 points, with clean turns and a clean landing. Holding cruise speed and climb height at this level across weaker days is what turns a strong round into a podium.

Recommendations

The recommendations that follow from the analysis, grouped by implementation theme and ordered by how much each would move Bill's score. Each theme links back to the evidence that motivates it and, where relevant, out to the matching Innovations tier.

  • Train faster inter-thermal cruise (top lever)
  • Bank more height per climb on weak days
  • Use more of the entry-speed cap
  • Tighten turnpoint lines (near a strength)
  • Audio vario and speech telemetry callouts, today

Cruise speed between thermals

Collapseback to top

Cruise pace between thermals is the single biggest lever. On clean laps Bill glides at 61.9 km/h against the same-air leader's 67.4 km/h, roughly 8% slower, at a shallower glide ratio (9.3 vs 10.3). That gap is about 90% of his 22 s per-lap clean-lap deficit, and a pace counterfactual attributes about +2.7 of the roughly three-lap shortfall to speed alone. Laps decide the score, so cruise pace is the underlying cause of the lower lap count (see the ranked phase levers in Analysis).

Drills

  • Speed-to-fly discipline: hold a higher glide speed between climbs and resist the instinct to stretch every glide flat.
  • Fly to a target inter-thermal cruise speed for the day's conditions rather than a habitual comfortable pace.
  • Cut altitude spent loitering at low value - convert height into distance while the air is sinking anyway.

Further analysis

  • Per-leg speed against wind direction once a task file with turnpoint coordinates is available, to separate true cruise pace from head/tail-wind legs.

Climb quality - height banked per thermal

Collapseback to top

Climb quality is the second lever, and it decides the weak days. Bill actually circles less than the leader in total (287 vs 402 s), so he is not over-thermalling; but he banks about 35% less height per thermal (40.7 vs 63.1 m) with wider, slower circles (39.4 vs 33.2 m radius; 0.89/2.55 vs 1.03/3.64 m/s mean/best climb). When lift is scarce this makes him land early - three laps in R9, two in R12 - which is where the lap-count shortfall opens up (phase levers; floor-vs-ceiling consistency).

Drills

  • Tighter, better-centred circles: work the core rather than orbiting it.
  • Bank-angle discipline - a consistent, committed bank to shrink the turn radius toward the leader's 33 m.
  • Commit to weak cores instead of leaving to search; patience before abandoning lift on poor-lift days.

Further analysis

  • Per-thermal centring traces (drift-corrected) to quantify how much of the height gap is radius versus core selection.

Where technology could help

A better real-time picture of climb rate and where the core sits is exactly what the navigator AR HUD and live AI cueing tiers target.

Entry speed - use the 120 km/h cap

Collapseback to top

Entry speed is a cheap early win. Bill crosses the start gate at 70.8 km/h against the leader's 94.5 km/h, leaving about 49 km/h of the 120 km/h cap unused - roughly twice the leader's unused margin. His entry altitude is already at the cap, so this is free opening-lap energy left on the table (see the entry-speed lever).

Drills

  • Build and carry start-gate speed up toward the 120 km/h cap on the run-in, so the first lap starts with the energy the rules allow.
  • Practise the timed dive-to-gate so the peak speed lands on the line, not before or after it.

Turnpoint lines

Collapseback to top

Turnpoint lines are already close to a strength - treat this as fine-tuning. Bill's lines run about 15 m per lap wider than the leader's, and turn technique costs only around 2 s per lap (about 10% of the deficit), the smallest of the four levers (phase levers, ranked).

Drills

  • Modest line tightening at the turnpoints, without bleeding the speed that the cruise lever is there to build - the two must not fight.

Rules-legal live signals

Collapseback to top

Several live aids are legal today and need no new rules. A pilot may field one navigator whose role includes relaying telemetry, and both an audio vario and spoken telemetry callouts are explicitly permitted. None of these feed data into control of the model, so they stay inside the Sport-class rules (the same permitted channel the live-cueing tier builds on).

Set up now

  • Audio vario tuning: shape the tone gradient tightly around the core so small changes in climb rate are audible, not just present or absent.
  • Speech telemetry callouts through the radio - climb rate, altitude band, distance-to-turn - so Bill keeps his eyes on the model.
  • A navigator working the ground station, calling the telemetry picture and the tactical decision points.

Resources

  • SM-Modellbau GPS-Logger 3 - logger with audio vario and speech telemetry output.
  • OLC-RC (Online Contest) - track upload and comparison for structured post-session review.
  • BMFA Silent Flight Technical Committee - GPS - the discipline's rules and equipment guidance.

Future extensions

These same permitted channels are the foundation the navigator AR HUD, live AI cueing and post-flight AI coach tiers extend.

Innovations

The art of the possible for coaching technology, ordered from the most tractable to the most ambitious. Each tier is framed against the Sport-class rules (regulations): passive telemetry display and relay are permitted and a navigator may relay them, but nothing may feed data into control of the model (section 2.7). Where a tier touches competition rather than training, the legality consideration is stated plainly.

  • Post-flight AI coach on this same data (most tractable)
  • Navigator AR HUD (organiser discretion)
  • Live cueing within the rules
  • A season-long data flywheel

Post-flight AI coach

Collapseback to top

A post-flight AI coach is the most tractable step, and this report is the proof of concept. The same pipeline that built this analysis can be pointed at any event or flight - straight from the open rcmodelspot data, or from an IGC log - to generate the round-by-round, phase-by-phase read automatically. On top of that it can drive a ghost replay of Bill against the same-air leader and flag recurring decision points, such as the glides where he consistently gives back cruise time or the climbs he leaves early.

Legality Consideration. No competition constraint: this is offline analysis of flights already flown, so it sits entirely in the training and debrief space. Track upload and comparison already exist through OLC-RC.

Navigator AR HUD

Collapseback to top

A navigator AR HUD re-presents telemetry that is already permitted, in a form that is faster to read. Climb rate, energy state, distance-to-turn, line deviation and a live thermal map could sit in the navigator's field of view instead of being read off a screen and spoken. Hardware matters here: today's Ray-Ban Meta glasses are audio and camera only with no display, so a visual HUD needs display-class glasses (for example Ray-Ban Display) or AR glasses such as Xreal or Rokid.

Legality Consideration. The regulations do not name AR or wearables. A navigator-worn HUD that only re-presents permitted passive telemetry - feeding nothing into control of the model - is plausibly legal at Contest-Director discretion; a pilot-worn HUD is safest treated as training-only until organisers rule on it (Sport-class regulations).

Live AI cueing

Collapseback to top

Live AI cueing turns the permitted speech channel into tactical calls. Telemetry streamed to a real-time engine could produce spoken prompts - commit to this core, push the glide, turn now - relayed by the navigator, plus a structured debrief the moment the flight lands. It is the natural extension of the audio vario and speech callouts that are already worth setting up today.

Legality Consideration. Spoken telemetry and an audio vario are explicitly permitted, and a navigator may relay them, so the audio path is legal in competition provided the cue is passive relay and nothing feeds into control of the model (regs section 2.7). The post-session debrief is unconstrained training use.

The data flywheel

Collapseback to top

A data flywheel compounds every flight into sharper coaching. Accumulating Bill's tracks together with the wider field's would support counterfactual what-if-you-had-stayed simulation on the climbs he left early, condition playbooks that map the day's weather to a tactical plan, and opponent profiling of how the strongest pilots handle weak lift. Each event ingested makes the next read better - the post-flight coach is the first turn of this wheel.

Legality Consideration. Purely offline and historical: no in-flight component, so no competition constraint. It depends only on the open track data already published per event.
